blocks.text: Imagine a spreadsheet where each row represents a unique entry, and each column represents a specific type of data. This is the essence of a relational database.

blocks.markdown: In the relational model, data is organized into tables, formally known as relations. Each table consists of rows, called tuples, and columns, known as attributes. Understanding the structure of these tables is crucial for effectively designing and querying databases.

blocks.title: Relation Schema
blocks.text: A relation schema defines a relation's name, its attributes, and the domain (data type) of each attribute. It is essentially the blueprint for a relation.

blocks.markdown: A relation schema is a formal description of a relation. It specifies the name of the relation and its attributes, along with the domains of these attributes. For example, a relation schema for a 'Student' table might include attributes like 'StudentID', 'Name', and 'EnrollmentDate', with respective domains such as integer, string, and date.

blocks.title: Tuple
blocks.text: A tuple is a single row in a relation, representing a single data item with values for each attribute.

blocks.markdown: In a relational database, each tuple is a unique instance of data that conforms to the schema. It contains values for each attribute defined by the schema. Importantly, in the relational model, a relation is a set of tuples, implying that duplicate tuples are not allowed.

blocks.title: Relations as Sets
blocks.text: Since a relation is a set of tuples, it cannot contain duplicate rows. Each tuple must be unique within the relation.

blocks.title: Defining a Relation Schema
blocks.prompt: Define a relation schema for a 'Book' table with attributes: 'ISBN', 'Title', 'Author', and 'PublicationYear'. Specify appropriate domains for each attribute.

steps.text: Identify the attributes and their data types.

steps.latex: Book(ISBN: string, Title: string, Author: string, PublicationYear: integer)

blocks.answer: The relation schema for the 'Book' table is Book(ISBN: string, Title: string, Author: string, PublicationYear: integer).

blocks.markdown: A schema is a structural definition, while an instance is a specific set of data conforming to that schema. The schema remains constant, but instances can change as data is added or removed.

blocks.title: Schema vs. Instance
blocks.prompt: Given a relation schema for 'Employee' with attributes 'EmployeeID', 'Name', and 'Department', describe an instance of this schema.

steps.latex: Employee(EmployeeID: integer, Name: string, Department: string)
\begin{array}{|c|c|c|} \hline EmployeeID & Name & Department \\ \hline 1 & Alice & HR \\ 2 & Bob & IT \\ 3 & Charlie & Finance \\ \hline \end{array}

blocks.answer: An instance of the 'Employee' schema could be a table with rows: (1, 'Alice', 'HR'), (2, 'Bob', 'IT'), and (3, 'Charlie', 'Finance').
